name: Scoring-robustness panel grid
summary: A grid of histograms crossing the paper's several invented interpretability scores against several populations of units — dictionary-learning features, MLP neurons, and features from a randomized transformer. It exists to show that the feature-over-neuron ordering survives every scoring choice, so no single panel is the result.
explanation:
### Why this chart and not another

Every interpretability score here is one the paper invented. There is no ground truth for "is this unit interpretable", so it builds several imperfect graders — a blinded human [[feature-interpretability-rubric]], [[automated-interpretability]] on activations, the same explanation checked against output weights — and trusts none on its own. What is being defended is not a number but an *ordering*: the [[feature|features]] found by [[dictionary-learning]] are more interpretable than the transformer's own MLP neurons, which are expected to be [[polysemanticity|polysemantic]]. A bar chart of medians would state the ordering but leave the obvious reply open: it holds only for the grader you picked. So one direction of the grid varies the scoring method and the other the population, and the result is that the ordering survives the crossing rather than sitting in one cell.

An average would also hide the shapes, where much of the argument lives. The distributions are skewed, spiky and sometimes bimodal: a tall column standing on zero correlation, because a constant prediction has no defined correlation and is scored zero ([[constant-prediction-zero-score]]); a second clump piled at the far right. A mean over that says little, which is why medians are marked with triangles.

### How to read it, step by step

In fig-69, rows are scoring methods and columns are populations, fixed all the way down: features from run A/1 ([[feature-notation]]), the MLP neurons of that same transformer, and features from a [[randomized-transformer]] whose weight matrices had their entries shuffled in place ([[weight-shuffling]]). Row 1 is the human rubric, $0$–$14$, in raw counts because the human sample is small; its unit is one scored [[activation-interval]], not a whole feature. Rows 2 and 3 are the *same* automated experiment scored twice, once with [[pearson-correlation]] and once with [[spearman-correlation]]; row 4 is [[automated-logit-scoring]], an accuracy where $0.5$ is chance. In rows 2–4 one bar is a bin of units, each contributing exactly one score, and height is density: each panel is normalised to area one, so populations of different sizes are comparable. The dotted vertical line is that row's null — zero correlation, or $0.5$ accuracy.

Colour in fig-69 is redundant, repeating the column. Read first *down* a column — does this population hold its shape under all four graders? — then *across* a row: does the left panel beat the middle? Rows 2 and 3 differ only in the coefficient, so compare them directly.

Fig-70 rotates the shape: population becomes colour — magenta A/1, yellow randomized, dark orange where they overlap — and the panels become the three scores, one of them split further by an inset.

### What a bad result would look like

The ordering flipping between rows 2 and 3, or holding under the automated graders but not the human one. Or medians that separate while the histograms sit almost on top of each other, so the gap is a summary statistic, not a real difference. Or the randomized column tracking the feature column everywhere, which would mean the decomposition recovers regularities of the dataset rather than anything the model computes ([[model-vs-data-question]]).

One cell does go the wrong way, and the paper leaves it in and labels it. On the activation score the randomized features take the higher median, roughly $0.62$ against $0.57$. This is the cell readers lift out and quote as a headline. The paper's answer is that the randomized model has more, and more strictly, [[single-token-features]], which are trivial to explain and so trivial to score; splitting that panel on the single-token property reverses the ordering ([[randomized-feature-bimodality]]). The split was chosen after the awkward result appeared, and the further claim — that what remains on the randomized side is no more interpretable than a polysemantic neuron — rests on the two distributions looking alike and on the authors' reading.

### Where it comes back

Fig-69 is the full four-by-three crossing, run mainly to show the Pearson-versus-Spearman choice does not make the result. Fig-70 narrows to two populations and the one cell that misbehaves, adding the single-token split as an inset. The importance-weighted rescoring in the next appendix section runs the same populations under one more correction to the grader, and there the gap narrows.
